claims.text: Dual-phase lamellar colonies contain numerous internal boundaries that promote microcracking during room-temperature tensile deformation.
A tailored post-processing heat and thermomechanical treatment can modify lamellar-colony interfaces.
The treatment can relieve stress concentrations at lamellar-colony interfaces.
The treatment can improve interfacial cohesion.
Improved interfacial cohesion and reduced stress concentrations can simultaneously enhance strength and room-temperature tensile ductility relative to the untreated alloy.
Modified lamellar-colony boundaries will promote crack deflection.
The post-processing treatment is expected to relax residual stresses.
The post-processing treatment may promote precipitate formation or controlled boundary refinement.
Adjusting interlamellar coupling will delay crack initiation.
Adjusting interlamellar coupling will deflect crack propagation.
Delayed crack initiation and deflected crack propagation will balance increased strength with improved ductility.
The treated alloy will exhibit a statistically significant increase in yield strength or tensile strength relative to the untreated baseline.
The treated alloy will exhibit a statistically significant increase in elongation at fracture relative to the untreated baseline.
Conventionally processed eutectic high-entropy alloys exhibit room-temperature brittleness because of microcracking at internal boundaries.
The beneficial treatment operates only within a narrow processing window.
Excessive treatment temperature or deformation could cause grain coarsening.
Excessive treatment could over-relax strengthening features.
Insufficient treatment may fail to modify the colony boundaries adequately.
Failure to improve both tensile strength and ductility significantly relative to an identically fabricated untreated control would falsify the hypothesis.
